title: AsyncIO & Concurrency: Threading vs Multiprocessing vs AsyncIO

slides.title: Concurrency Paradigms in Python
slides.prompt: Python supports three main concurrency models: Threading (for I/O-bound tasks with shared memory), Multiprocessing (for CPU-bound tasks bypassing the GIL), and AsyncIO (cooperative multitasking using single-threaded event loops).
slides.codeSnippet:
# Concurrency Selection Matrix:
# - I/O-bound (Network/Disk) -> AsyncIO or Threading
# - CPU-bound (Data Crunching/Math) -> Multiprocessing

slides.title: GIL Definition
slides.prompt: Fill in the acronym name for Python's mechanism that prevents multiple native threads from executing bytecode simultaneously.
slides.codeSnippet: The ___ (Global Interpreter Lock) restricts CPython thread parallelism.

slides.title: Optimal Concurrency Model for CPU-bound Tasks
slides.prompt: Which concurrency model should be chosen for heavy numerical computation tasks in CPython?

slides.title: AsyncIO Task Switching Mechanism
slides.prompt: How does AsyncIO achieve multitasking within a single thread?
options: Cooperative multitasking where tasks yield control explicitly using await
Preemptive multitasking managed by the OS kernel scheduler
Time-slicing bytecode instructions via GIL signals
slides.correctAnswer: Cooperative multitasking where tasks yield control explicitly using await

slides.title: Shared Memory in Multiprocessing
slides.prompt: Do separate processes in the `multiprocessing` module share memory space by default?
options: No, each process has its own isolated memory space and interpreter instance
Yes, all processes share global variables automatically
Yes, but only for immutable data structures
No, unless running on Windows operating systems
slides.correctAnswer: No, each process has its own isolated memory space and interpreter instance
